name: Industrial carbon capture and storage
summary: Industrial CCS captures concentrated carbon dioxide from a plant and transports it to monitored geological storage.
useCase: A cement plant sends captured process emissions through a shared pipeline or ship terminal to an offshore storage site under a long-term service contract.
whyNow: Global CCS Institute reported 77 operating commercial facilities in its 2025 assessment, up from 50 a year earlier. The count demonstrates more operating infrastructure, but it is not a direct measure of CO₂ actually stored: plants differ in size and utilisation. Another 47 facilities were under construction. Shared transport and storage hubs can help smaller emitters join the market, provided liability, permits and service contracts are clear. Point-source CCS is separate from direct air capture, and captured CO₂ used in a short-lived product should not automatically be counted as permanent storage. The attractive commercial unit is an integrated, funded chain from capture through verified storage.

mainstream.scope: Routine contracting for selected cement, chemicals and other industrial sources that can access viable shared transport and permanent-storage hubs.
mainstream.rationale: Capture has operating precedents, but repeat deployment for hard-to-abate industrial emissions requires storage availability, permits and durable revenue. Projects now under construction can support a broader service market in the early 2030s. This window does not imply CCS on most factories or power stations; high total-chain costs and unbuilt storage can push projects past 2035.

metric.name: Operating commercial CCS facilities
metric.scope: Global CCS Institute commercial facility universe; includes different industrial sectors and facility sizes.
metric.limitations: Facility counts do not measure tonnes captured, permanent storage or utilisation. The Institute’s broader development pipeline is not operating capacity, and its definitions differ from other CCUS databases. The 2025 report’s total 513 Mt/year pipeline must not be represented as actual capture.
metric.futureNote: No defensible comparable external deployment forecast found. The separate maturity path is an analyst scenario, not measured adoption.

milestones.text: Commercial capture predates this window; no comparable annual facility observation was retained from the selected recent assessment.
Carbon Clean raised a reported $150 million to scale capture technology; financing is an innovation signal, not tonnes stored.
No harmonised annual operating-count observation retained here; the maturity path reflects commercial niche use rather than a measured penetration rate.
The 2025 Global CCS Institute comparison uses 50 operating facilities as its prior-year baseline.
Global CCS Institute reported 77 operating facilities and 47 under construction in October.
IEA refreshed its CCUS project database in March; project-by-project status is more useful than treating the entire announced pipeline as operating.

tailwinds: Some industrial process emissions are difficult to eliminate through electrification alone.
Shared pipelines, shipping terminals and storage sites can spread infrastructure cost.
Existing subsurface engineering capabilities can support storage development and monitoring.
bottlenecks: Capture, transport and storage must all be ready, financed and contractually connected.
Energy requirements and total-chain cost can be high for dilute or small sources.
Long-term liability, permits, measurement and storage acceptance require durable institutions.
watchMetrics: Actual annual CO₂ permanently stored, separately from nameplate capture capacity.
Construction progress and contracted emitter volumes at storage hubs.
Total cost per verified tonne avoided, including energy use, upstream emissions and transport.
